title: Carpenters and a cooper come ashore at Baile dhìreach
summary: A boat of the humans' post rows down from Cuan shean deep with sawn plank and grounds on the shingle north of the quay at Baile dhìreach. Seven men of Harrow's ships come ashore, the carpenter William Rook and the cooper Samuel Hale among them, seeking a sheltered beach for a slip where the small craft of the post may be mended and built.

title: The rule of the shingle read to the strangers
summary: The shingle above the wrack-line at Baile dhìreach is held in keeping for the whole town and may not be sold. Seonag nic Aoidh of the salt-house reads the town's rule to the strangers on the shore: the well drawn in turn, no fire on the shingle in the herring season, no hammer on the rest-nights. Rook says his men will keep it.

title: The first human house on the shingle
summary: The carpenters of Baile dhìreach lay a slip of split logs, raise an open shed, and build a house of sawn plank on a sill of beach stones, with a window of glass. Since nothing may be built on the shingle, the town rules that the house is a tent, and calls it so. The humans' book of the town enters it as the first house.

title: Samuel Hale tightens the herring barrels
summary: The human cooper Samuel Hale takes down the leaking herring barrels of Baile dhìreach stave by stave and makes every one of them tight by the end of summer, beginning with the idle row of the salter Ruairidh. He takes a bowl from the pot for his pay, and asks for Dia-thìris words, which he writes under his own.

title: The first boat off the humans' slip
summary: On the first evening of Lùnastal the humans' slip at Baile dhìreach launches a small coaster of the strangers' pattern, deeper in the keel than the boats of the south-west. She is built for the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim, paid for in fish and labour and rigged with the town's rope; his wife pours sea water on her bow and asks Manannan to keep her.

title: Two letters on the harbour of Baile dhìreach
summary: The humans' post at Ros dhomhain writes to ask why the dues of a harbour its own men have half rebuilt go wholly to the custodians at Cathair dhearg. The custodians of Inis thais write to ask by what rule strangers keep a yard on a shingle held in keeping. Iain mac Chaluim says the town must write its rule down.

title: The compact written in both tongues
summary: Through the moons of harvest six sit at the mending-table in the net-loft of Baile dhìreach, three of the town and three of the strangers, and write the town's rule twice. A clerk of Inis thais writes the Dia-thìris book and William Rook the humans'. The net-maker Eilidh nic Ruairidh and the cooper Samuel Hale are fetched to find the words for the moorings.

title: The chair set to turn at the humans' new year
summary: The six of Baile dhìreach find that the town's year turns at Samhain and is counted by moons, while the humans' year turns in the dead of winter on a fixed day. They write in both books that Iain mac Chaluim holds the chair until the humans' year turns, and William Rook for the year after, and so in turn.

title: The first dues shared
summary: At its first sitting the council of six of Baile dhìreach settles a quarrel over a mooring ring and sends the harbour dues out in two halves: one in a sack by a boy up the road to the custodians at Cathair dhearg, the other round by boat to the humans' post at Ros dhomhain.

title: Ruairidh refuses the cooper
summary: On the night of Samhain, while the town keeps its fire on the headland above the quay and the humans watch from the last cairn, the cooper Samuel Hale comes to the door of the salter Ruairidh to ask for his daughter Eilidh nic Ruairidh. Ruairidh sends him away, saying that a council is one thing and a hearth another.

title: The bidding carried to Inis thais
summary: In the black moon the council of Baile dhìreach sends its compact along the shore to the temple city of Inis thais in both tongues, with a clause bidding any town of the coast sit with it on the same terms. The pilot Murchadh mac Iain carries it by boat and brings back word that the custodian will write.

title: A stranger's prayer at the lamps of the drowned
summary: At the dark of the year Baile dhìreach sets lamps along its quay for its drowned, as the harbours of the west do. The humans of the shingle stand in the line, and the cooper Samuel Hale says a prayer to Crìosd in his own tongue for shipmates lost in the northern sea on the voyage out. Eilidh nic Ruairidh sets a lamp for them.

title: Iain mac Chaluim hands the chair to William Rook
summary: On the morning the humans' year turns, in the net-loft of Baile dhìreach, the fisherman Iain mac Chaluim gives up the chair of the council of six and the carpenter William Rook takes it, as the compact bids. Both books enter it in a line, the one by the day and the year, the other by the moon. The letter from Inis thais is read the same morning.

title: Rook's ruling on the dragged mooring
summary: A boat of the post drags her anchor at Baile dhìreach and fouls the salter Ruairidh's mooring, and her master will not pay. William Rook, in the chair, orders his own countryman to pay the town's rate for rope and ring, in iron by weight, that day, and asks Ruairidh whether the rate is fair.

title: The storm of the wolf-moon at Baile dhìreach
summary: A three-day storm off the west drives the sea over the quay of Baile dhìreach and up the shingle towards the boats. On the second night the town and the humans haul the boats over the crest together with ropes, blocks and a capstan-bar from the slip. The salt-house chimney and half the roof of the humans' house are lost.

title: Ruairidh relents
summary: After half a moon of the carpenter in the chair, in which nothing in Baile dhìreach has fallen but a chimney, the salter Ruairidh helps the humans roof their house again and sends word by his daughter Eilidh nic Ruairidh that the cooper Samuel Hale may come up to the house for his bowl himself.
